notes: Collins J dismisses police officers' JR challenging bad-faith disciplinary proceedings and suspension after Stoner prosecution stayed.

enrichment.short_title: Ashton v West Yorkshire: judicial review of police disciplinary proceedings after abuse of process stay

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: PCs Ashton and Fraser arrested David Stoner in Leeds on 21 March 2003 during Cross Green disorder; their statements and the CPS prosecution alleged s.5 public order conduct not supported by video evidence.
The Stoner prosecution was abandoned and both officers were charged with attempting to pervert the course of justice; HH Judge Gullick stayed that prosecution as an abuse of process.
The officers remained suspended and faced Police (Conduct) Regulations disciplinary charges of dishonestly fabricating evidence to justify the arrest.
They sought judicial review alleging bad faith by the Professional Standards Department and unlawfulness of their continuing suspension.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Chief Constable's decision to continue disciplinary proceedings and maintain suspension after the criminal prosecution was stayed.
enrichment.outcome: Both claims dismissed; disciplinary proceedings may proceed and suspension was lawful, though suspension paperwork was inadequate and reasons should be given on request.
enrichment.ratio: Allegations of bad faith in police disciplinary proceedings require positive proof; a prima facie disciplinary case may proceed even where a related criminal prosecution was stayed for abuse of process, and suspension pending dishonesty charges is lawful where charges remain live.
legal_issues: Whether disciplinary proceedings were pursued in bad faith against PCs Ashton and Fraser
Whether continuing suspension after the criminal stay was unlawful
Whether Regulation 9 notices should have been served before further statements were sought
Whether reasons for suspension must be given to the officer
catchwords: attempt to pervert the course of justice

confidence.notes: Final dismissal, disciplinary rationale and suspension findings are clearly reasoned.

notes: Leveson J awards modest assault damages against acquitted defendant who misidentified murder victim's house; balance of probabilities standard applied.

enrichment.short_title: Shah v Gale: civil liability after wrongful-house identification leading to fatal stabbing
key_facts: Naresh Shah was fatally stabbed at 41 Hibernia Road, Hounslow on 9 March 2002 after doormen attacked the wrong house seeking Xhafer Ismaili.
Kelly Gale had pointed out 41 Hibernia Road rather than Ismaili's home; Jason Grant was convicted of murder and others of conspiracy to cause GBH, but Gale was acquitted.
Shah's estate sued Gale for battery and conspiracy, seeking modest damages for the assault rather than dependency or fatal accident losses.
Gale admitted misidentifying the house but denied knowing grievous harm was intended.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of civil claim for assault damages following acquittal in the criminal proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Claim partly succeeded; Gale liable for joint-enterprise assault but not for knife use or fatal injuries; total award £2,750 plus aggravated damages.
enrichment.ratio: Civil claims for serious criminal conduct are proved on the balance of probabilities with cogent evidence, not the criminal standard; a defendant who knowingly identifies a victim's home for a retaliatory attack may be liable in tort for the assault even if acquitted of conspiracy to cause GBH, but is not necessarily liable for a knife attack outside the scope of the joint enterprise.
legal_issues: Whether the civil standard of proof applies to allegations of assault causing death
Whether Gale was party to a joint enterprise to assault the occupant
Whether criminal acquittal precluded civil liability
Admissibility and weight of police interviews excluded under PACE section 78 in the criminal trial
linked_authorities: Re H and R (Child Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) [1996] 1 FLR 80
Francisco v Diedrick, The Times, 3 April 1998
Halford v Brookes, The Times, 3 October 1991

confidence.notes: Standard of proof, liability findings and damages award are all explicit.

notes: Newman J finds GP breached duty on second Christmas Day visit in meningococcal septicaemia case; first visit not below standard.

enrichment.short_title: McDonnell v Holwerda: GP standard of care in suspected meningococcal infection in a child
key_facts: Sebastian McDonnell, aged 4½, developed meningococcal septicaemia on Christmas Day 1997 causing amputation of his right leg and digits.
Dr Holwerda visited twice after the family called her out; on the second visit the child had photophobia, rash, vomiting and irritability.
The GP treated for gastroenteritis and did not refer the child to hospital; he was admitted later that night after fitting.
Experts agreed earlier referral would have led to antibiotic treatment between about 10.30 pm and 11.00 pm.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of liability and limited causation issues in a clinical negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on the second visit; the GP's hasty assessment fell below the standard of a reasonably competent GP, though the first visit did not breach the standard.
enrichment.ratio: A GP must assess the aggregate of symptoms and signs in a febrile child and refer on a properly formed suspicion of meningococcal infection without waiting for classical meningism; rigid exclusion of photophobia, rash and irritability can breach the duty of care even where individual signs appear non-specific.
legal_issues: Standard of care when a GP sees a child with high fever and possible meningococcal infection
Whether failure to refer on the first visit was negligent
Whether failure to refer on the second visit was negligent
When the claimant would have received hospital treatment if referred

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings on both visits and clear liability conclusion on the second occasion.

notes: Kay and Steyn LJJ dismiss cocaine conspiracy appeals; cut-throat trial management and Randall relevance analysis upheld.

enrichment.short_title: R v Dunn and Gonzalez: cut-throat defences and cross-examination under the Criminal Evidence Act 1898
key_facts: Dunn and Gonzalez were convicted at Maidstone of conspiracy to supply about 2 kg of cocaine after a handover at the Dartford Hilton car park.
Dunn gave evidence of an alleged remand confession by Gonzalez, losing his shield under section 1(3)(iii) and exposing both to extensive cut-throat cross-examination.
Gonzalez was refused permission to adduce propensity evidence against Dunn on firearms, Bradford drugs and money laundering matters.
Both received nine-year sentences; co-accused Turner pleaded guilty and Tabares was acquitted by direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction following a joint trial with cut-throat defences.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; convictions held safe.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant gives evidence against a co-defendant under section 1(3)(iii), cross-examination on unproven charges is permissible if relevant to credit; propensity evidence between co-defendants requires rigorous relevance analysis under R v Randall and mere arguability is insufficient.
legal_issues: Permissible scope of cross-examination after a defendant gives evidence against a co-defendant
Whether severance was required mid-trial because of prejudice to Dunn
Whether Gonzalez could adduce propensity evidence against Dunn
Whether exclusion of Gonzalez's proposed propensity evidence was correct
linked_authorities: R v B (C) [2004] 2 Cr App R 34
R v H and C [2004] 2 WLR 335

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on each contested evidential ruling is comprehensive and explicit.

notes: Owen J declares unlawful detention of disputed-age asylum seekers at Oakington after supportive paediatric age reports.

enrichment.short_title: I and O v SSHD: unlawful detention of age-disputed unaccompanied asylum seekers
key_facts: Two asylum seekers, I and O, claimed to be 16 but were treated as adults and detained at Oakington fast-track centre.
Consultant paediatrician Dr Michie assessed both as aged 17 plus or minus two years, consistent with their claimed dates of birth.
The Secretary of State maintained detention pending Cambridgeshire Social Services age assessments, which later confirmed both were under 18.
I was detained unlawfully from 22 to 27 January 2005 and O from 22 to 28 January 2005 after Dr Michie's reports were received.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of continued detention of age-disputed minors after receipt of expert paediatric age assessments.
enrichment.outcome: Claim allowed; declaration that detention for the specified periods was unlawful; matter transferred to the Queen's Bench Division for damages assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a consultant paediatric age assessment with a plus or minus two year margin supports a claimed minor status, the Secretary of State must apply his own policy and give the benefit of the doubt; irrationally preferring a later social services assessment while rejecting equivalent expert evidence renders continued detention unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Michie's reports amounted to credible medical evidence requiring release under IND policy
Whether the five-year margin of error in Royal College guidelines invalidated the expert reports
Whether continued detention after the reports was irrational
Whether there was any rational basis for preferring CSS assessments to Dr Michie's reports
linked_authorities: R (B) v Merton London Borough Council [2003] 4 All ER 280

confidence.notes: Policy analysis, irrationality finding and declaration of unlawful detention are clearly stated.

notes: Court of Appeal upholds service out on XL Specialty as necessary party to Carvill reinsurance brokerage dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Carvill v XL Specialty: service out of jurisdiction on reinsured in brokerage dispute
key_facts: Carvill brokers sued European reinsurers for unpaid brokerage under excess of loss and excess cession reinsurance treaties.
XL Specialty Insurance, the US-based reinsured, applied to set aside service out of the jurisdiction.
Permission to serve XL had been granted on the basis XL was a necessary or proper party to the existing claim.
XL argued there was no serious issue against it and that the English court lacked a proper basis for jurisdiction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court refusal to set aside an order permitting service of the claim form on XL out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Where a reinsured may bear ultimate liability for brokerage owed to the broker and the dispute requires one investigation of liability across the reinsurance chain, the reinsured may be a necessary or proper party to proceedings against reinsurers and service out of the jurisdiction may properly be permitted.
legal_issues: Whether there was a serious issue to be tried against XL on the merits
Whether XL was a necessary or proper party to the claim against the reinsurers
Whether the order for service out of the jurisdiction should be set aside
Whether one consolidated investigation of European brokerage liability was required

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional reasoning is detailed though some treaty merits issues remain for trial.

notes: Coulson J grants summary judgment enforcing adjudicator's decision for shopfitting sums at Bucklers Hard property.

enrichment.short_title: Allen Wilson Shopfitters v Buckingham: summary enforcement of construction adjudication award

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998
Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: Allen Wilson Shopfitters carried out over £500,000 of refurbishment works at Mr Buckingham's property at Clobb Copse House, Bucklers Hard.
The parties disputed the contractual basis of the works after the contract administrator was dismissed in January 2005.
An adjudicator decided that £50,401.35 was due for valuations 12 and 13, plus interest, RICS nomination fee and adjudicator's fees.
Mr Buckingham, acting in person, challenged jurisdiction and argued the JCT adjudication clause was unfair under consumer regulations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application for summary judgment to enforce an adjudicator's decision under CPR Part 24.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted for the claimant for £50,401.35, interest, the RICS nomination fee and £2,112.25 plus VAT in adjudicator's fees.
enrichment.ratio: In adjudication enforcement proceedings the court does not generally revisit the merits of the underlying contractual dispute; if the adjudicator had jurisdiction under the contract and the notice of adjudication, the decision must be enforced unless there is a clear defence.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator had jurisdiction despite dispute over the written contract
Whether termination of the contract administrator affected adjudication jurisdiction
Whether the consumer unfair terms regulations invalidated the JCT adjudication clause
Whether any defence existed to enforcement of the adjudicator's decision

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction analysis and enforcement order are clearly reasoned despite underlying contract uncertainty.

notes: Laddie J refuses VCI leave to join BHB and plead Article 82 abuse over horseracing pre-race data pricing.

enrichment.short_title: BHB v Victor Chandler: database rights and alleged abuse of dominance over pre-race data
key_facts: The British Horseracing Board compiled extensive pre-race data used by bookmakers and had earlier sued William Hill for unauthorised use.
Victor Chandler International sought to amend its defence and join BHB and Press Association in a Part 20 claim alleging abusive pricing.
VCI contended BHB charged excessively for pre-race data, breaching Article 82 and the Chapter II prohibition.
The Board's data income funded regulatory and industry functions benefiting the horseracing sector as a whole.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications for leave to join additional defendants and to amend pleadings to allege abuse of dominant position.
enrichment.outcome: Applications refused; no permission to join BHB or PA or to plead Article 82/section 18 abuse; interim injunction application fell away.
enrichment.ratio: A dominant undertaking's freedom to contract and set prices requires careful justification before competition intervention; high prices alone, without evidence of unfair pricing or exclusionary abuse, do not establish a viable Article 82 or Chapter II case.
legal_issues: Whether BHB held a dominant position in pre-race data
Whether pre-race data pricing was an abuse of dominance
Whether VCI should be permitted to join BHB and Press Association
Whether an interim injunction should be granted
linked_authorities: British Horseracing Board Ltd v William Hill Organisation Ltd (C-203/02) [2004] ECR I-10415

confidence.notes: Interlocutory competition ruling is clear though full merits of database claim are not finally resolved.

notes: Lawrence Collins J grants summary judgment on pension scheme partnership deed claim against Kean Hird and associated defendants.

enrichment.short_title: Repton Pension Trustees v Hird: summary judgment on SDP special partner partnership deed
key_facts: Trustees of the Repton Securities Directors Pension Scheme sued over a Partnership Deed funding a £400,000 special partner interest in the South Downs Partnership property venture.
Kean Hird and associated Frame companies invested through the pension scheme structure managed by James Hay Pension Trustees.
The defendants resisted the claim and counterclaimed, alleging an overarching partnership and estoppel.
The claimants applied for summary judgment under CPR Part 24 on the Partnership Deed claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery Division summary judgment application on the claim and parts of the counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted for the claimants; no real prospect of successfully defending the Partnership Deed claim; partnership to be dissolved subject to limited retention of legitimate expenses.
enrichment.ratio: Where a written Partnership Deed clearly governs a pension-funded special partner investment and no viable estoppel or variation case is pleaded, the court may grant summary judgment and order dissolution without a full trial.
legal_issues: Whether the Partnership Deed bound the parties and entitled the pension trustees to the investment proceeds
Whether an overarching partnership existed outside the deed
Whether estoppel or variation prevented reliance on the Partnership Deed
Appropriate remedy including dissolution and retention of legitimate partnership expenses

confidence.notes: Summary judgment reasoning is explicit though final order on retained expenses was subject to further argument.

notes: Sir Andrew Morritt VC holds British Museum cannot restitute Nazi-looted drawings absent legislation; Attorney-General questions answered negatively.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney-General v British Museum: restitution of Nazi-looted Old Master drawings
key_facts: Four Old Master drawings in the British Museum were claimed by the heirs of Dr Feldmann as stolen by the Gestapo in Brno in March 1939.
The Trustees wished to return the drawings but were constrained by the statutory prohibition on disposing of collection objects.
The Attorney-General brought Part 8 proceedings asking whether moral obligation or the Snowden jurisdiction could authorise transfer.
A Spoliation Advisory Panel later recommended legislation to permit restitution of Nazi-era looted objects.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 claim by the Attorney-General seeking the court's determination of questions as to the Trustees' power to dispose of museum objects.
enrichment.outcome: Questions 1(a), 2 and 3 answered in the negative; Trustees have no power to restitute the drawings without legislation or a bona fide compromise of title.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3(4) of the British Museum Act 1963 absolutely prohibits disposal of collection objects except under specified statutory exceptions; moral obligation, public policy or the Attorney-General's Snowden jurisdiction cannot override that prohibition, and only Parliament can authorise restitution.
legal_issues: Whether section 3(4) prevents restitution of spoliated collection items
Whether moral obligation can justify disposition outside statutory exceptions
Whether the Snowden jurisdiction enables transfer despite section 3(4)
Whether a bona fide compromise of the heirs' title could authorise restitution

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and final answers to the Attorney-General's questions are comprehensively reasoned.
